failures.title: BMW S63B44 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Tensioner Wear - The S63's Primary Weakness
items.whatHappens: Like its N63 sibling, the S63B44 uses a timing chain tensioner that can weaken over time, allowing chain slack. This can lead to rattling on cold start, timing drift, and eventually catastrophic valve‑to‑piston interference if the chain jumps. The S63 is more robust than the N63, but the tensioner remains a known wear item - especially on early 2010-2012 production engines.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early (rattle only, before timing codes appear), tensioner and guide replacement is a manageable repair (£1,500-£2,500). However, if the chain has jumped and valves have contacted pistons, the engine is typically beyond economical repair - a full replacement is the only safe option. Read our full timing chain failure guide

items.title: Hot‑Vee Related Failures - Valve Stem Seals & Turbo Coolant Lines
items.whatHappens: The S63's hot‑vee design places the turbos inside the V of the engine, creating extreme heat. This accelerates wear on valve stem seals (leading to oil consumption and blue smoke on start‑up) and causes plastic coolant lines around the turbos to become brittle and crack. While the S63 uses improved materials over the early N63, these are still common failure points.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve stem seal replacement is a labour‑intensive job (£3,000-£5,000) and requires specialist tooling. Coolant line replacement is cheaper but often done at the same time. If oil consumption is excessive or the engine has overheated due to coolant loss, a reconditioned unit may be more cost‑effective than a full repair. Read our full oil consumption guide

items.title: Turbocharger Wear - Wastegate Rattle & Bearing Play
items.whatHappens: The S63's twin‑twin‑scroll turbos are under constant high‑temperature stress. Wastegate bushings wear, causing rattle on deceleration, and turbo bearings can develop play, leading to reduced boost and oil consumption. This is more common on high‑mileage examples or cars that have been aggressively tuned.
items.repairVsReplace: Turbo refurbishment or replacement is a specialist job (£1,500-£3,000 per turbo). If both turbos are failing and the engine is out for other work, many owners opt for a full reconditioned unit with refreshed turbos already included.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the S63B44
variants.intro: The S63B44 is the M‑division twin‑turbo V8, closely related to the N63 but featuring forged internals, higher boost, and M‑specific calibration. It is distinguished from later variants by its 555-560 hp output and specific engine management hardware. Where the code appears: - Stamped on a metal plate on the engine block (left‑hand side, near the timing cover) - On the V5C logbook under "Engine number" (the first 7 characters will read S63B44) - Via BMW VIN decoder - the 7th character of the VIN indicates engine type Commonly confused with: - N63B44A - the non‑M 4.4L twin‑turbo V8; shares the block but lacks forged internals, has different turbos and lower output (400-450 hp) - S63B44A - later M V8 variant with 575 hp (found in F10 M5 LCI, F06 M6 LCI) - S63B44T0 - another variant used in F10 M5 Competition Package - S63B44T2 / S63TU - the Technical Update family found in F90 M5, G‑series M5/M8, F95 X5M, F96 X6M

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement S63B44 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used S63B44 can be a viable option if it comes from a low‑mileage, well‑maintained car with full service history. However, this engine is often subjected to hard use - without proof that the timing chain tensioner has been addressed and the turbos are in good health, a used unit is a gamble. Many used S63 engines are sold with known issues. Factor in £2,000-£4,000 for preventative work (tensioner, valve stem seals) if the history is unclear. Link once: /services/used-engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper S63B44 recon is the gold standard for M5/M6/X5M/X6M owners. A quality recon should include: full strip and inspection, new timing chain tensioner and guides, refreshed valve stem seals, replacement of all plastic coolant lines, turbo refurbishment, new gaskets and seals, and a full test. With a 12-24 month warranty, this gives you a fresh engine with all known weaknesses engineered out - well worth the £9,000-£14,000 supply cost for a high‑value M‑car. Link once: /services/reconditioned-engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified when the original engine has suffered catastrophic failure (chain jump, seized turbos, overheating) and the car is a low‑mileage collector or cherished daily driver. An upgraded rebuild should include forged pistons, upgraded rod bearings, a reinforced timing chain guide, and a full cylinder head overhaul. This is specialist work and typically only makes sense for cars with strong residual value (£25,000+). Link once: /services/rebuilt-engines

items.question: What are the most common failures on the S63B44?
items.answer: The most documented issues are timing chain tensioner wear (causing cold-start rattle and potential chain jump), hot-vee heat-related failures (valve stem seals leading to oil consumption, and cracked plastic coolant lines), and turbocharger wear (wastegate rattle, bearing play). Tensioner replacement is strongly advised at 60k-100k miles as preventative. Valve stem seal replacement can cost £3k-£5k - often done alongside other work. Turbo refurbishment is common on high-mileage examples.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned S63B44 engine?
items.answer: A used S63B44 can be viable if it has full documented history and proof of tensioner and turbo condition. However, these engines are often driven hard; without evidence of preventative work, a used unit carries significant risk. A reconditioned engine is the safer choice - it typically includes new tensioner, refreshed valve stem seals, replaced coolant lines, and turbo refurbishment, with a 12-24 month warranty. Used is cheaper (£5k-£9k) but factor in £2k-£4k for preventative work. Reconditioned addresses all known weak points and gives peace of mind.

items.question: How do I confirm my car has the S63B44 and not another BMW V8?
items.answer: Check the engine code stamped on the block (left-hand side near the timing cover) - it will read S63B44. The V5C logbook also lists the full engine number, with the first 7 characters identifying the code. Common confusions: N63B44 (non-M, lower output), S63B44A (later 575 hp variant), and S63TU (F90-generation). Fitting a later TU engine into an early chassis is not a straight swap - ECU, wiring and cooling differ.

items.question: How long does an S63B44 engine typically last?
items.answer: With meticulous maintenance and early preventative work, these engines can exceed 120,000 miles. The forged internals are robust, but the limiting factors are the timing chain tensioner and hot-vee heat stress. Tensioner and guide replacement recommended at 60k-80k miles. Strict adherence to 5,000-mile oil changes with BMW M-spec oil is critical. Regular inspection of coolant lines and valve stem seals extends lifespan.
